prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose imagination, with poetry as its ground, that turns memory, the body and dream into a sustained metaphysical architecture and renews the novel's means.

statement.case_for: My preferred laureate does not change: Mircea Cărtărescu (B024). Round 1 produced no new evidence about the texts, so I will not treat the exchange as a reason to move, and I do not count the shared first place as an argument. The case rests on the common criteria. The voice is unmistakable in long, intricately patterned sentences and recurring imagery of the body, memory and cosmology. As I understand public knowledge, Blinding and Solenoid show formal control at very large scale. The imaginative and intellectual depth is built into the architecture of the books and is not applied as decoration. The oeuvre is long enough to be judged as a whole. On the chair's questions, I would test the maturity claim by asking whether Solenoid, as the later large work, opens an imaginative space that the Orbitor project did not, or only enlarges it. I read the public record as suggesting development, but I cannot verify that. Evidence against it would be a consistent critical account that the late books recycle the early imagery without raising the stakes. On citation scope, I now prefer wording that names prose as the core and poetry as its ground, as Palm proposes. I drop the phrase 'European tradition of inward and fantastic narrative' that I used in round 1. It adds a regional frame that the literary argument does not need, and it comes close to the national or regional symbolism several of us want to avoid. A citation that names form and imagination is cleaner and easier to defend.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged and is evidential. The case rests on Romanian sentence rhythm, long-sentence control and register, and I cannot confirm how much of that survives translation. I have not independently read the originals. The unevenness of the longest books is a live possibility that nobody in the exchange could verify. My coverage of the early poetry and the essays is thinner than my coverage of the novels. The 'poetry as its ground' wording therefore claims more than I can fully support, and I would accept 'prose' alone if colleagues judge the poetry too thinly covered. If the committee concluded that sustained quality is concentrated in a few peaks, or that the late work only repeats the early architecture, the case would weaken. Adonis would then deserve the closest look, because his achievement lies in a formal renewal of a poetic language. Carson would be next.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu first on the coherence and scale of the oeuvre. She states a test that would weaken her own case, namely that quality might be concentrated in a few peaks. She ranks Adonis fourth because poetry suffers most in translation and she wants Arabic-reading assessments to carry real weight.
responses.response: I take her peaks test as the right one for Cărtărescu and I apply it to my own judgment. I cannot show that the quality is spread across the body of work, only that the public record points that way. Her translation caveat on Adonis is the one I press hardest on myself. I ranked him second, but my reading of the achievement is second-hand, and I cannot say whether my confidence is larger than my evidence. We agree that Arabic-language assessments are what would settle the question. Without them, Adonis stays an alternative for me, not a first choice. That asymmetry also works against Cărtărescu, since I judge him through translation too, and it is why I keep stating the dependence.

responses.point: Palm frames the citation as fiction at the core with 'poetry as its ground'. She answers the breadth worry by saying the project joins the intimate to the encyclopedic and reaches across poetry and prose. She also says she is the wrong judge of Adonis's formal achievement in translation and objects to age entering the discussion.
responses.response: Her citation wording is the one I now prefer, because it names the core without claiming that the poetry is equal in weight to the novels, which I cannot support. Her answer on breadth is persuasive as an account of how the project is built. It is still an argument about the works' intent and architecture, and it does not show that the effect reaches beyond readers of ambitious fiction. I keep that as an open question. On Adonis I agree that age and timing are not literary criteria and I give them no weight. I raised timing in round 1 only as a practical remark, not as a ground for preferring him, and I withdraw it from the substantive discussion.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Cărtărescu first for a singular idiom and keeps Carson as an alternative, asking whether her hybridity is a core achievement or a series of brilliant experiments. He also leaves open how the will's reference to an idealistic tendency applies to an inward, encyclopedic and often disturbing project.
responses.response: On Carson I think the answer depends on the committee first agreeing the core. If the original poetry, verse narrative and essays are the core and the classical translations and scholarship are context, her case is easier to state, but I still cannot show that sustained quality holds beyond Autobiography of Red and Nox. That is why she is my second alternative and not higher. On the will, I share his unwillingness to treat the reading as settled. I would read the idealistic tendency in terms of what a body of work attempts in its imaginative and moral ambition, and not as a test of tone or comfort. On that reading Cărtărescu's project, which tries to make an inner life carry a whole cosmology, is not disqualified. I hold that as an interpretation open to correction, not as a finding.

responses.point: Mattson frames the Cărtărescu citation around prose and the novel's imaginative and formal means. She keeps Murnane as an alternative for restraint, precision and self-scrutiny, while granting that his narrow range makes the claim to wide significance harder. She also says Adonis's poetic achievement should be kept apart from his role as cultural theorist.
responses.response: I agree with her on keeping Adonis's poetry apart from his role as theorist and public figure, and my citation logic for any Adonis case would run through the poems and the critical prose about poetic language. On Murnane, I accept her point that narrowness is not a flaw in itself and that intensity is a legitimate literary quality. My difficulty remains the criterion of significance across a body of work. His plain English prose is less exposed to translation loss than Cărtărescu's, which is an advantage in judging him. But I still find the imaginative range smaller than that of the candidates I rank above him, so I keep him sixth. Her prose-centred wording is close to mine, and I differ only on whether to name the poetry as the ground.

responses.point: Swärd keeps Yan Lianke as her first alternative on narrative form and the poetics of mythorealism. She ranks Adonis seventh because his main formal influence may belong to earlier decades and she cannot judge his recent sustained quality. She says she would reconsider if colleagues who can speak to the Arabic originals argued for it.
responses.response: Her request for evidence about recent sustained quality in Adonis is fair, and I cannot meet it from what is available to me. I rank him high on the strength of his formal and linguistic renewal, and a renewal that belongs mostly to earlier decades is a different claim from sustained achievement across the whole oeuvre. That is a real weakness in the case I have been making. On Yan Lianke, I agree that the invention of a grotesque and mythic narrative mode is a literary achievement. The corpus remains uneven in translation and circulation, and nobody has shown that the quality holds across the large body of titles. I therefore still keep him outside my two alternatives, though on narrative form alone I take her case more seriously than my fifth place suggests.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's verbal texture, sentence rhythm and long-sentence control survives in translation; all judgment here rests on public knowledge and reception, not independent reading of the Romanian originals.
Whether the later very long novels deepen the early project or only extend it; the exchange produced no new evidence either way.
How thinly the early poetry and essays are covered in translation, and so whether the 'poetry as its ground' wording is supportable or should be reduced to prose.
Whether the committee has access to Arabic-language assessments that could settle what translation hides in Adonis, and whether his sustained quality extends to recent decades.

Whether Carson's hybrid works and classical translations constitute one sustained oeuvre, and how the will's reference to an idealistic tendency applies to Cărtărescu and Carson; I treat my reading as an interpretation, not a finding.
I have not independently verified any work, critical consensus or bibliographic detail discussed in this exchange.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. The supplied profile records no connection to any shortlisted writer. I note that my own writing on Central Europe and its history concerns a region adjacent to Romania. It is context only, and I have deliberately removed the regional framing from my proposed citation so that it does not shape the wording. The profile also records that I was elected to the Academy together with Ingrid Carlberg. This is an institutional connection between members and has no bearing on any candidate. These disclosures are not adjudicated.
